item.title: NZ special-vote history threatens National’s narrow majority, putting Fiji-born Wong in kingmaker spotlight
item.description: New Zealand’s history of special-vote counting has raised questions about whether Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s narrow parliamentary majority will survive the final election results, potentially placing Fiji-born Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong in a decisive kingmaker position. item.content:encoded:
New Zealand’s history of special-vote counting has raised questions about whether Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s narrow parliamentary majority will survive the final election results, potentially placing Fiji-born Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong in a decisive kingmaker position.

Saturday’s general election left National and its coalition partners, ACT and New Zealand First, with a projected 67 seats in a 131-seat Parliament, just above the 66-seat majority threshold. Labour and its potential governing partners, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori, secured a projected 57 seats, while Opportunity gained seven.

The Electoral Commission’s preliminary results, released on Sunday, show that approximately 399,365 special votes, including 96,947 overseas and dictation votes, remain to be checked and counted. Special votes require additional eligibility checks, with the official results expected on Friday, 27 November, potentially changing the parliamentary balance.

National lost two seats between election night and the official count in each of the last three general elections, according to Electoral Commission records.

In 2023, its allocation fell from 50 to 48 seats, following similar reductions from 35 to 33 in 2020 and 58 to 56 in 2017.

Special votes accounted for 603,257 ballots, or approximately 21 percent of votes cast, in 2023, compared with around 17 percent in both 2020 and 2017. The estimated 399,365 special votes in the current election represent approximately 14 percent of the anticipated total vote.

If National’s coalition loses a net two seats in the current election and Parliament remains at 131 members, its projected majority would disappear, leaving it with 65 seats.

Such a shift could make Wong’s seven projected MPs crucial to negotiations over the next government, although historical voting patterns do not guarantee a similar outcome this year.

Special votes changed government arithmetic in 1999

The 2017 election provides a striking precedent. Although National won more seats than Labour, special votes reduced its parliamentary allocation from 58 to 56, while Labour gained one seat and the Greens another. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters subsequently chose to support a Labour-led government, enabling Jacinda Ardern to become Prime Minister despite National remaining the largest party.

A significant precedent occurred in 1999, when special votes deprived the Labour–Alliance coalition of its projected parliamentary majority.

The coalition finished with 59 seats in the 120-member Parliament, while the Green Party gained seven seats after initially securing none in the election-night allocation.

Labour and the Alliance subsequently formed a minority coalition government.

Born in Fiji to a Chinese father and Pākehā mother, Wong, 38, moved to New Zealand when she was six months old and grew up in Auckland. Her parents met while studying at university in New Zealand.

She is poised to make electoral history as the first party leader without prior parliamentary experience to lead a party into Parliament under New Zealand’s Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system.

Her Opportunity Party received 144,298 votes, or 5.96 percent of the preliminary party vote, securing seven list seats.

Opportunity’s potential influence will depend on the official results and whether either major political bloc needs its support to form a government.

Wong has indicated she is willing to negotiate with either bloc, although Luxon has previously ruled out governing with Opportunity because of disagreements over its tax proposals.

Opportunity’s economic proposals could have implications for Tongan households, particularly those facing rising living costs and housing pressures.

The party proposes a Citizen’s Income of up to NZ$370 a week for eligible adults, replacing several existing welfare benefits.

It also advocates an annual land-value tax of 1.75 percent on urban land and 0.5 percent on rural land, aimed at discouraging land banking and improving housing affordability.

Opportunity claims its wider reforms would improve household finances and reduce house prices, although the financial impact would vary depending on household circumstances and property ownership.

Whether any of these proposals become government policy could depend on Opportunity’s influence in the next Parliament.

The Electoral Commission is expected to release the official election results on 27 November, following the counting of special votes.
